newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: EU says it got 98 percent of what it sought in ITA.
newsitem.headline: EU says it got 98 percent of what it sought in ITA.

text.p: The European Union obtained all but a fraction of its initial objectives in the Information Technology Agreement, but the fate of the pact was still in doubt as late as Thursday morning, EU officials said.
Peter Carl, the bloc's chief ITA negotiator, said he was unsure when EU trade ministers met early on Thursday morning whether they would approve the deal he had hammered out with the United States.

"And the reason for this is very simple. Some of our trading partners were holding out against the inclusion of some of the most significant products used in the information society and this was not acceptable to the majority of member states," Carl told a news conference.
His disclosure helps explain an outburst just before the EU meeting by acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, who said she did not know whether the EU was committed to an ITA.

Carl, who called the negotiations "short but arduous", said the breakthrough came when the United States and Japan -- with whom EU and U.S. negotiators were in intense contact -- agreed to the EU's requests for broader product coverage.

Japan agreed on Thursday afternoon to include copper cables -- a basic component of telecommunications equipment -- and special chemicals used in the manufacture of semiconductors in the plan to scrap IT tariffs by the year 2000, Carl said.
The European Commission said Washington eventually covered 70 percent of the trade volume it had earlier sought to exclude.

"This, together with the EU's support for the other products in the agreement, means that the EU has achieved about 98 percent of its initial objectives in terms of trade coverage," the Brussels-based executive said in a statement.
EU trade in IT goods totals well over $100 billion a year, with imports outstripping exports by about two to one.
Carl said IT exports to the EU from Asia and the United States could well double in the next five years as a result of the deal, deepening the EU's trade deficit in the sector.
But he said: "That is a matter of total indifference to us."
Far more important was the reduction in costs to business, and hence to consumers, that the ITA would bring about, he said.
Carl said there were no EU-Japan side agreements in the accord similar to the EU-United States deal to scrap tariffs on cognac, whiskey, gin and vodka.
